slides.title: Why aerial fiber doesn't fall
slides.sub: Strand and lashing, explained in 9 slides

slides.title: Fiber can't hold its own weight.
slides.body: The cable has very little tensile strength. A steel wire above it does the real work.

slides.title: The strand carries the load
slides.body: Galvanized steel, usually 7 wires twisted together, tensioned pole to pole to a designed sag. US sizes: 6.6M and 10M.

slides.title: Lashing ties cable to strand
slides.body: A machine rides the strand and spirals thin stainless wire around both. Heavier bundles get two wires: double lashing.

slides.title: Overlashing: the big shortcut
slides.body: Route already has lashed copper or coax? Lash the new fiber onto that bundle. No new strand, often a simpler permit.

slides.title: Not every country does this
slides.body: Strand and lash is the US default. India leans on figure-8 cable with a built-in steel messenger. Australia uses both.

caption:
Fiber cable can't hold up its own weight. So what keeps it in the air?

A steel messenger strand takes the load, and a thin stainless lashing wire spirals the cable onto it. Swipe for the parts at the pole, the 7-step build, and why overlashing often means a simpler permit.
